bib.title: AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents. Xuan Zhang, Longtao Zheng, Cunxiao Du, Bo An, Xin Dong. Preprint, arXiv:2610.02163v1, 1 Oct 2026.

COVERAGE: 41,304 of 41,304 chars (11 pages). Nothing skipped. References were read for origins only.

CLAIMS
- claim: Trained AutoCompact (SFT then RL) has the highest full-run pass rate on both benchmarks, 9.2 and 5.0 points above Base.
  number: 39.6% vs 30.4% (SWE-bench Verified); 24.5% vs 19.5% (SWE-PolyBench Verified)
  setup: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, one terminal REPL scaffold, 256K window, no cost cap, averaged over three runs
  quote: "AutoCompact Learned SFT→RL 256K 39.6 24.5" and "Base — — 256K 30.4 19.5"
  where: p6, Table 1

- claim: Length-triggered compaction at 16K scores below full history at 256K, and RL on a length trigger recovers only a little.
  number: Fixed 28.8/18.6; CompactionRL 32.7/19.8
  setup: same model and scaffold, 16K forced-compaction threshold. These baselines use a different context setting from the 256K rows.
  quote: "Fixed Compaction Length — 16K † 28.8 18.6" and "CompactionRL (Li et al., 2026b) Length RL 16K † 32.7 19.8"
  where: p6, Table 1

- claim: Like for like at the shared 16K threshold, AutoCompact beats Base at every budget, and this is the paper's only same-window test of proactive vs. length-only compaction with RL.
  number: 38.0% vs 28.8%; +44 to +55 tasks per 500
  setup: SWE-bench Verified, both with forced fallback; AutoCompact may also compact early
  quote: "+55 +44 +44 +46 +46 +46\n28.8%\n38.0%\n(c) AutoCompact vs. Base, 16K with fallback"
  where: p6, Fig. 3c

- claim: Actually executing compaction helps most under tight budgets, and the advantage shrinks at high budgets.
  number: 19.9% at $0.10; 1.9% at $4.00; 39.6% vs 37.7% at the top budget
  setup: same trained checkpoint with compact() calls skipped (Summary-ignored), SWE-bench Verified
  quote: "The advantage is 19.9% at $0.10 and remains 1.9% at $4.00, so executing compaction improves cost efficiency without reducing final performance."
  where: p8; 37.7% from Fig. 3d, p6

- claim: Prompting alone does not produce proactive compaction in the base model.
  number: Base rate ≈0% (Fig. 4a)
  setup: preliminary experiments with compaction rules in the agent prompt
  quote: "While Base rarely invokescompact(), AutoCompact-SFT already uses it on 44.3% of tasks"
  where: p3-4 for the prompting statement; p7 for the quote

- claim: RL raises compaction use and cuts summary omissions, with no compaction-specific reward.
  number: use 44.3% to 58.5%; key-state omissions 3.1% to 0.2%; next-action omissions 8.2% to 2.2%
  setup: all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, keyword-based screening plus random manual spot checks
  quote: "RL extends its use to 58.5% of tasks while reducing both types of summary omission: key-state omissions fall from 3.1% to 0.2%, and next-action omissions fall from 8.2% to 2.2%."
  where: p7

- claim: Most of the stacked gain comes from RL, not from judge-guided SFT.
  number: SFT 32.2/21.7; RL adds 7.4 and 2.8 points
  setup: 256K; RL on SWE-Gym with binary task reward, jointly over coding and compaction
  quote: "Outcome-based RL then improves pass rates by a further\n7.4% and 2.8% over AutoCompact-SFT on the two benchmarks."
  where: p7

- claim: Proactive compaction helps even when nothing overflows, including an untrained rubric and SFT-only methods.
  number: SelfCompact 31.7/20.6; SWE-Compressor 31.0/20.1; AutoCompact-SFT 32.2/21.7; Base 30.4/19.5
  setup: 256K, no trajectory reaches the forced threshold in the Fig. 3a comparison
  quote: "SelfCompact (Li et al., 2026a) Rubric — 256K 31.7 20.6"
  where: p6, Table 1; the interpretation is "These results suggest that proactive context management helps even when the full history fits in context." (p6)

- claim: Executing corrections online beats inserting compaction calls offline into finished trajectories, which keeps the original follow-up actions. The authors say "suggests".
  number: 1.2 and 1.6 points
  setup: AutoCompact-SFT vs SWE-Compressor, same model and scaffold, comparable training data
  quote: "AutoCompact-SFT exceeds\nSWE-Compressor by 1.2% and 1.6% on the two benchmarks."
  where: p6

- claim: Most corrections target what the summary keeps, ahead of when to compact and how to continue.
  number: 1,052 trajectories from 379 tasks; 24% trigger, 53% working state, 23% continuation
  setup: SWE-rebench, GPT-5.5-Codex as judge, removed at evaluation; malformed requests, summary loops and off-track continuations were filtered out
  quote: "Of these trajectories, 24%\nsupervise compaction triggers, 53% supervise working-state construction, and 23% supervise post-\ncompaction continuation."
  where: p5

- claim: A summary can keep the state and name a next action yet still contradict itself ("summary self-consistency"). The SFT summary recorded an unresolved syntax error but proposed finishing, and that run failed.
  number: none (one task, django-13809, paraphrased summaries)
  setup: qualitative case study; the authors say the difference "may stem from" training objectives
  where: p8, Section 3.4, Fig. 5

Method facts for the note (no quote needed beyond the number above):
- Compaction replaces earlier history with a summary headed `# Auto Context Summary`, keeping the original task unchanged (p3). Related Work describes the result as the summary "alongside the original task and recent turns" (p9).
- The three supervised decisions are trigger, working state and continuation (p4).
- All tokens in a trajectory share one advantage across segments split where the prefix is rewritten (p4).

LIMITS
Conceded by the authors:
- RL trained on 32K-token sequences while evaluation used a 256K window (p9).
- A single scaffold was studied. The authors leave combining learned compaction with Codex or Claude Code as future work; they only say the 16K results "suggest" it could help (p9).
- Summary-omission rates rest on keyword screening plus spot checks, not full annotation (p7).

Not shown by the paper:
- No confidence intervals or significance tests. Results are three-run averages, and one base model was used throughout.
- Costs are estimates from token usage at Alibaba Cloud pricing, with cached tokens at 20% of input rate (p5). There is no measured latency.
- Only coding benchmarks are covered, and no safety-rule or constraint retention is measured.
- RL is joint over coding and compaction, so its 7.4 points are not attributable to compaction alone.

My observations against the target note (for your decision; nothing edited):
- All the note's AutoCompact figures match the source (39.6, 30.4, 28.8, and the quote).
- The note compares 39.6% (256K) with 28.8% (16K), which crosses windows. The like-for-like 16K pair is 38.0% vs 28.8%.
- At the top budget, the Summary-ignored checkpoint still scores 37.7%, against 30.4% for Base. So at full budget about 7.3 of the 9.2 points survive with compaction calls skipped. That qualifies the note's line that "Dropping stale context is worth doing for quality". The clean no-overflow evidence for that is smaller: SFT at +1.8 and SelfCompact at +1.3.
- SelfCompact, a rubric with no training, beat Base by 1.3 and 1.1 points, so "prompting alone does not get it there" is the authors' preliminary finding, not a universal result. The paper does not reconcile the two.

BUILDS ON
- CompactionRL (Li et al., 2026b), SelfCompact (Li et al., 2026a), SWE-Compressor / "Context as a tool" (Liu et al., 2026)
- SWE-MeM (Gao et al., 2026), concurrent work
- GRPO (Shao et al., 2024); multi-turn RL, SimpleTIR (Xue et al., 2026)
- REPL scaffold: Lin & Liu, 2025; Du et al., 2025
- Data and benchmarks: SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025), SWE-Gym (Pan et al., 2025), SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024), SWE-PolyBench (Rashid et al., 2025)
- Also credited for context management: MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), ACON (Kang et al., 2026), ReSum (Wu et al., 2025), Context-Folding (Sun et al., 2025), AgentFold (Ye et al., 2025)

CODE: None worth keeping. The paper prints no code or prompts, only the action name `compact()` and the summary header `# Auto Context Summary` (p3).

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p2, "Length-triggered compaction versus AutoCompact": side-by-side trajectories show a seam-based trigger against a limit-based one, faster than prose.
- Fig. 2, p3, "Judge-guided on-policy data collection": shows the keep, replace and repair corrections and that the corrected output is what executes.
- Fig. 3, p6, "Pass rate versus inference budget on SWE-bench Verified": four panels. Panel (d) shows the execution benefit narrowing as budget rises, and panel (c) has the like-for-like 16K result.
- Fig. 4, p7, "Compaction behavior": three small bars for the when, what and how metrics across Base, SFT and RL.
- Fig. 5, p8, "Summary self-consistency on SWE-bench Verified task django-13809": a compact visual of a summary contradicting itself.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction runs some words together (for example "invokedcompact()", "AUTOCOMPACT: LEARNINGWHEN TOCOMPACT") and hyphenates at line ends. Quotes are kept as extracted, with \n marking line breaks.
- The prompting sentence spans a page break between p3 and p4.
- Figure 3 values come from extracted chart labels, not a table. The mapping of labels to series comes from panel order, so check 38.0% and 37.7% against the figure image before printing them.
- No embedded instructions found.

Tools used: Read, Bash, and SubagentHandback for this report; no tool I needed was refused.
